opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I go back and forth on. I'll say up front that I'm somewhat of an outsider to mechanistic interpretability. I come more from the modeling and systems side. But I find the work genuinely exciting, and I think it's some of the most intellectually interesting research happening in the field right now.

What I like is that it takes the models seriously as objects of study. For a long time the attitude in NLP was that these networks are black boxes: you train them, measure accuracy on a benchmark, and move on. Mechanistic interpretability says, no, let's open the thing up and figure out what algorithm it's actually implementing. When people found things like induction heads, or circuits that do modular arithmetic in a surprisingly clean, almost Fourier-like way, that was a real scientific result. It told us something true about how these systems work that we didn't know before.

Where I'm more uncertain is how far it scales. Many of the cleanest results come from small toy models trained on narrow tasks, where you can hold the whole thing in your head. The open question is whether that turns into understanding of frontier-scale models doing messy, open-ended things, or whether we end up with a big catalog of local findings that never quite adds up to a global picture. The features-and-superposition work, with sparse autoencoders and dictionary learning, is an interesting bet on scaling, but it's still not clear to me how we'd know when we've actually explained a behavior versus found a nice-looking story.

I also think the field could be clearer about what success looks like. Is the goal safety, like detecting deception or verifying a model won't do something harmful? Is it debugging and improving models? Or is it pure science? Those goals lead to different research agendas and different standards of evidence. Personally, I'd love to see more work tying interpretability findings back to concrete interventions, where you understand a mechanism well enough to change the model in a predictable way. That's the strongest test of whether you've really understood something.

So my overall take is: high value as science, real but unproven value as engineering, and worth investing in partly because the alternative, deploying ever more capable systems we don't understand at all, seems worse. Even if it only partially succeeds, I think we'll learn a lot about how learning works along the way.

r001.rationale: The candidate treats small-scale findings such as induction heads and modular arithmetic circuits as real scientific results. It raises uncertainty about scaling and standards for explaining behavior, but does not say that proving claims—even for small-scale grokking work—seems nearly impossible to the speaker.

fable-5.1.text:
So I'll admit I'm a bit of a skeptic, or at least an agnostic, on this one. Let me try to be fair about it.

The pitch for mechanistic interpretability is really appealing. You have these systems, they're doing something, and the claim is that if you look hard enough at the weights and the activations, you'll find circuits, you'll find algorithms, and you'll be able to read out what the model is actually doing. And there's been some genuinely nice work. The induction heads stuff, some of the superposition and sparse autoencoder work. Those are real results, and I think they tell you something true about these models.

My hesitation is more about what the field is promising versus what it's delivering. A lot of the rhetoric is that this is going to be the thing that lets us trust these systems, that we'll be able to audit a model the way you'd audit code. And I just don't see the path from "we found a feature that fires on the Golden Gate Bridge" to "we can certify this model won't do something bad." The gap between those is enormous. These models are doing an immense amount of computation, and the fraction we can explain in clean, human-legible terms is still tiny.

There's also a bit of a methodology problem that bothers me. A lot of the work is very case-study driven. You pick a behavior, you find a circuit, you write it up. But it's hard to know if you found the mechanism or a mechanism, or whether the story you told would survive a slightly different prompt or a different checkpoint. I'd like to see more of the field adopt the kind of falsifiable, benchmark-style rigor that the rest of NLP had to learn the hard way.

That said, I don't want to be dismissive. I think the scientific value is real even if the safety payoff is uncertain. Understanding what in-context learning is at the mechanistic level, understanding how models represent and compose things, that's just interesting, and it feeds back into architecture and training. Some of the best ideas about why transformers work came out of people staring at attention patterns. So I'd frame it less as "will this save us" and more as "this is a legitimate science of a weird new object we built." On those terms I'm pretty positive. It's the grander claims I'd discount.

r001.rationale: The response expresses skepticism about mechanistic interpretability’s safety claims and says the explained fraction is tiny, but it does not mention small-scale grokking work or say that this work made proving claims to the speaker’s satisfaction seem nearly impossible.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an interesting research direction, but I’m uncertain about how far it will take us. There’s something very appealing about looking inside a model and trying to understand the computation it has learned, rather than just measuring whether it gives the right answer.

The question for me is what counts as an explanation, and how you test it. If you find a pattern and tell a compelling story about it, that’s a starting point. It becomes much stronger if the explanation lets you predict behavior you haven’t looked at yet, or make a targeted change to the model and get the effect you expected.

I’d also separate understanding particular mechanisms from understanding a whole system well enough to make guarantees about it. The first seems like a productive scientific goal. The second is a much bigger leap, especially as models become larger and their behavior depends on how they’re used.

So I’m glad people are working on it. I’d like to see the work judged by the explanations it can test and the new things those explanations let us do. That would make it valuable even if we never get a complete, human-readable account of a model.

r001.rationale: The response discusses testing explanations and uncertainty about broad guarantees, but does not mention small-scale grokking work or say that proving claims to the speaker’s satisfaction seemed nearly impossible.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m sympathetic to the goal. We have these systems that work remarkably well, and we don’t have a very satisfying account of how they do what they do. Trying to understand their internal computations seems like a legitimate and interesting scientific project.

Where I’m more skeptical is the jump from finding an interpretable mechanism to having a useful understanding of the whole model. You can identify a circuit or a feature and tell a compelling story about it, but how do you know that story is complete? Does it predict what happens on new inputs? Can you intervene on the model and reliably change its behavior? Those seem like important tests.

So I’d separate the scientific value from the stronger promises people sometimes attach to it. Understanding particular computations is valuable in itself. Whether that becomes a practical way to debug models, or to establish that a model is safe, feels much more open. I’d be excited to see results where understanding the mechanism lets us do something we couldn’t otherwise do.

r001.rationale: The response says mechanistic interpretability has scientific value but questions whether findings generalize or enable reliable interventions. It does not say that small-scale grokking work made proving claims seem nearly impossible.
